h1: Mileage Reimbursement Calculator California Rules and State Laws
cardBlurb: Understand how California labor code requires employer vehicle expense payments while Texas and Michigan rely on federal minimum wage baselines.
introText:
California requires employers to reimburse employees for all necessary vehicle costs from driving on the job. Texas and Michigan set no state-specific mileage reimbursement requirement at all. At ModernWallet, we build financial models and calculators to help workers understand how federal mileage figures differ from mandatory employer pay. Many drivers mistakenly assume federal tax benchmarks automatically dictate payroll reimbursements across the entire country.

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) sets standard mileage rates primarily for self-employed taxpayers calculating Schedule C deductions. For 2026, the federal rate is 72.5 cents per mile from January 1 through June 30, and 76 cents per mile from July 1 through December 31. That rate was 70 cents per mile for the entirety of 2025. While federal tax law establishes these numbers to measure vehicle operating costs, it does not force any private employer to pay them to W-2 staff.

Understanding your rights requires looking at the specific employment statutes in your state. A worker running a mileage reimbursement calculator California search needs to navigate California Labor Code Section 2802, whereas an employee in Texas or Michigan must look to federal minimum wage baselines.

sections.heading: Employer Reimbursement Rules Versus Federal Tax Deductions
sections.body:
The federal mileage rate set by the IRS functions as an optional benchmark for tax deductions rather than a universal mandate for employee paychecks. When self-employed contractors compute their annual tax filings, they use the [IRS standard mileage rates](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/standard-mileage-rates) to claim business travel deductions on Schedule C. For calendar year 2026, the rate is 72.5 cents per mile for travel from January 1 through June 30, and 76 cents per mile for travel from July 1 through December 31. During calendar year 2025, the rate stood flat at 70 cents per mile.

Federal statutory law contains no general rule requiring private employers to pay these rates to their W-2 employees. Companies frequently choose to adopt the federal number for convenience because payments up to that rate qualify as non-taxable expense reimbursements under an accountable plan. When an employer chooses not to provide reimbursement, federal tax law does not intervene to penalize the business unless employee wages drop below statutory wage floors.

This separation between tax deductions and payroll obligations catches many workers off guard. If your company pays zero cents per mile, you cannot look to the IRS to demand a check. You must examine the labor laws in your state or check whether your out-of-pocket costs reduce your pay below the federal minimum wage. For tracking federal write-offs, you can test scenarios using our [mileage deduction calculator](/mileage-deduction/).

sections.heading: California Labor Code Section 2802 and Vehicle Expenses
sections.body:
California mandates full employer reimbursement for all necessary expenditures employees face when operating personal vehicles for work tasks. Under [California Labor Code Section 2802(a)](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2802.), an employer must indemnify an employee for all necessary expenditures or losses incurred in direct consequence of the discharge of duties. Section 2802(c) defines these expenditures to include all reasonable costs, which means workers cannot be forced to absorb gasoline, wear and tear, auto insurance, or maintenance on work assignments.

California administrative bodies and state courts interpret this statutory requirement to cover work-related travel beyond the standard daily commute. Employers have several lawful options to satisfy their indemnity obligation under the statute:

- Pay an agreed per-mile rate that covers operating costs, which frequently mirrors the federal IRS rate.
- Reimburse the actual recorded expenses of the employee, supported by fuel receipts, maintenance bills, and insurance statements.
- Provide a regular lump-sum travel stipend or vehicle allowance structured to fully absorb anticipated driving expenses.

No matter which payment system a business implements, the payment must actually cover the worker's reasonable operating costs. The federal IRS mileage rate serves as a practical, widely adopted benchmark in California workplaces, but the statute does not name it as an inflexible ceiling or legal floor. If an employee shows that their actual operating costs exceed the standard per-mile payment, the employer remains responsible for the difference. Furthermore, Section 2802(c) establishes that an employee who prevails in a legal claim for unreimbursed expenses is entitled to recover reasonable attorney fees.

sections.heading: Texas Mileage Rules and the Federal Minimum Wage Floor
sections.body:
Texas labor statutes contain no mandatory requirement for private employers to reimburse employees for personal vehicle expenses or business travel. Private businesses in Texas are permitted to set their own travel reimbursement policies, offer a partial per-mile allowance, or decline to reimburse mileage altogether. A worker in Texas who uses a personal car for deliveries, customer visits, or site inspections cannot cite a state-level labor code provision to compel payment.

The legal protection available to Texas employees comes instead from the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). Under the FLSA, personal vehicles used for business duties are treated as tools of the trade. If an employer requires a worker to supply a vehicle without reimbursement, those vehicle operating expenses cannot reduce the worker's net earnings below the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour in any given workweek.

The Texas state minimum wage matches the federal rate of $7.25 per hour, which has remained unchanged since July 24, 2009. Under the wage kickback principle outlined in [U.S. Department of Labor Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2009-2](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/field-assistance-bulletins/2009-2), an expense required by the employer cannot kick back into the minimum wage floor. For instance, if an hourly delivery driver in Texas earns $10.00 per hour across a 30-hour week ($300.00 gross) and incurs $100.00 in vehicle expenses, their net pay drops to $200.00, or $6.67 per hour. Because $6.67 sits below the $7.25 federal floor, that unreimbursed driving creates an actionable FLSA minimum wage violation.

sections.heading: Michigan Minimum Wage Laws and Unreimbursed Driving
sections.body:
Michigan law does not establish a state-mandated mileage reimbursement rate for private-sector employers. Similar to Texas, Michigan leaves travel reimbursement policies to the discretion of private employment contracts and company handbooks. A private company in Michigan has no statutory obligation to pay the federal IRS rate or reimburse vehicle wear, provided the policy does not violate basic wage protections.

Protection against excessive unreimbursed driving costs in Michigan operates through the state's minimum wage floor. Under Michigan's Improved Workforce Opportunity Wage Act, the state minimum wage rose to $13.73 per hour effective January 1, 2026, according to the [Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity](https://www.michigan.gov/leo/news/2025/12/08/michigans-minimum-wage-set-to-increase-on-jan-1-2026). Because Michigan sets its statutory baseline significantly higher than the federal $7.25 rate, employers face state-level wage claims when out-of-pocket vehicle expenses erode worker earnings.

The FLSA anti-kickback principle applies in Michigan alongside state wage rules, but the higher state floor changes the arithmetic for workers. An employee earning $16.00 per hour in Michigan who drives extensive unreimbursed miles would experience an unlawful wage reduction once their net pay drops below $13.73 per hour. The legal issue in Michigan remains centered on wage floor protection rather than an explicit statutory right to mileage reimbursement.

sections.heading: The Department of Labor Standard for Reasonable Approximations
sections.body:
Federal labor regulators do not require employers to track actual vehicle expenses or pay the official IRS rate to stay compliant with wage standards. The United States Department of Labor (DOL) confirmed in [Wage and Hour Division Opinion Letter FLSA2020-12](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WHD/opinion-letters/FLSA/2020_08_31_12_FLSA.pdf) that employers may reimburse personal vehicle expenses through a reasonable approximation of costs. Any appropriate method that reasonably reflects operating burdens satisfies federal statutory obligations.

This official guidance clarifies that the FLSA does not mandate the IRS standard business mileage rate. An employer who pays a custom per-mile sum, a fixed weekly gas stipend, or a flat monthly travel allowance complies with federal law as long as the net wage does not fall below the legal minimum wage. Workers cannot force a company under federal jurisdiction to switch to the 2026 IRS rate of 72.5 or 76 cents per mile if the employer's chosen formula reasonably covers driving costs.

For workers in states like Texas and Michigan, this opinion letter limits the ability to demand higher mileage rates. Unless your net earnings drop below the governing minimum wage, your employer possesses broad authority to establish reimbursement amounts. Only states with affirmative indemnity statutes, such as California, give workers the legal right to challenge reimbursements that fall short of actual, reasonable costs.

sections.heading: Steps for Workers Addressing Unreimbursed Business Miles
sections.body:
Workers who believe their employers are shorting vehicle payments should document their business driving records before initiating a dispute. Maintain a detailed contemporaneous travel log that records trip dates, starting locations, work destinations, client purposes, and exact odometer readings. Keep all fuel receipts, maintenance invoices, and vehicle insurance renewal notices to establish an accurate record of your real operating costs.

Your path to resolution depends entirely on the state where you perform your work:

- In California, present your records to your payroll or human resources department and reference California Labor Code Section 2802. If the company refuses to indemnify your reasonable expenses, you can file a wage claim with the California Labor Commissioner or pursue a civil action, which permits the recovery of attorney fees under Section 2802(c).
- In Texas, review your gross weekly earnings and compare them to your estimated vehicle expenses to verify whether your net hourly pay falls below $7.25. If unreimbursed driving pushes your compensation below minimum wage, you can file an FLSA wage complaint with the federal Department of Labor.
- In Michigan, calculate your net earnings against the state minimum wage of $13.73 per hour. When out-of-pocket driving costs drag your effective pay below that threshold, submit a complaint to the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity or federal wage authorities.

Workers employed across international borders face distinct national tax systems and vehicle allowances. If you manage remote staff or drive outside the United States, consult our guide to [international mileage reimbursement rates](/guides/mileage-reimbursement-rates-uk-canada-ireland-nz/) for details on travel rules in the United Kingdom, Canada, Ireland, and New Zealand.

sections.heading: Independent Contractors and Self-Employed Mileage Filings
sections.body:
State expense reimbursement statutes and federal minimum wage protections apply exclusively to bona fide W-2 employees. If you work as an independent contractor or 1099 gig worker, your client or platform is not required to reimburse your vehicle expenses under California Labor Code Section 2802 or the FLSA. Gig workers driving for food delivery or rideshare applications must absorb vehicle depreciation, maintenance, and fuel as personal business costs.

Independent contractors recover these vehicle operating expenses through federal tax deductions on Schedule C rather than employer expense checks. You can learn how to compute these write-offs by reading our guide to the [DoorDash mileage deduction](/mileage-deduction/doordash-mileage-deduction/) or reviewing our detailed analysis of the [2026 split IRS mileage rate](/mileage-deduction/irs-mileage-rate-2026/). Deducting business miles lowers your net business earnings, which in turn reduces your liability for both income tax and self-employment tax.

Contractors who miscalculate their business miles risk overpaying self-employment taxes on their annual returns. To estimate your tax obligations and plan quarterly estimated payments accurately, calculate your potential liability with our [self-employment tax calculator](/self-employment-tax/).

faqs.question: Does my employer have to pay the IRS mileage rate in California?
faqs.answer: California employers are not legally required to use the specific IRS mileage rate, but they must reimburse all reasonable and necessary vehicle expenses under California Labor Code Section 2802. Many employers choose to pay the federal IRS rate because it serves as an established benchmark that satisfies state indemnity rules without triggering payroll taxes. If an employer chooses a lower rate or a monthly stipend, the payment must still cover the worker's actual operating costs.

faqs.question: Is Texas required to reimburse mileage?
faqs.answer: Texas state law does not require private employers to reimburse employees for mileage or personal vehicle use. The only legal constraint comes from the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, which prevents unreimbursed work expenses from dropping an employee's effective hourly pay below the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour. If your net hourly wage stays above $7.25, a Texas employer can legally decline to pay mileage.

faqs.question: Does Michigan require employers to reimburse mileage?
faqs.answer: Michigan does not have a state statute mandating mileage reimbursement for private-sector workers. However, Michigan employers must comply with the state's minimum wage under the Improved Workforce Opportunity Wage Act, which set the wage floor at $13.73 per hour effective January 1, 2026. If unreimbursed business driving reduces an employee's net hourly earnings below $13.73, the employer faces a wage violation.

faqs.question: What is the 2025 IRS mileage rate compared to 2026?
faqs.answer: The IRS standard business mileage rate was 70 cents per mile for all of calendar year 2025. For calendar year 2026, the IRS enacted two separate rates: 72.5 cents per mile for travel between January 1 and June 30, and 76 cents per mile for travel between July 1 and December 31. These federal rates apply to self-employed tax deductions and serve as non-taxable reimbursement benchmarks for employers.

faqs.question: What can I do if my employer won't reimburse my mileage?
faqs.answer: First, maintain an accurate, contemporaneous mileage log tracking trip dates, business destinations, miles driven, and vehicle operating receipts. If you work in California, you can request full indemnification under California Labor Code Section 2802 or file a formal claim with the California Labor Commissioner. If you work in Texas or Michigan, determine whether your unreimbursed costs push your net pay below the applicable minimum wage floor, and file a wage claim with state or federal labor authorities if a violation exists.
